desc:
In one move you choose one index and then add 1 to every other element (all elements except the chosen one). Return the minimum number of moves needed to make all elements of nums equal.

For example, [1, 2, 3] needs 3 moves: [1,2,3] → [2,3,3] → [3,4,3] → [4,4,4].
hints: Simulating the moves is hopeless for large values. Look for what a single move does to the differences between elements.
Raising all elements except one by 1 changes the differences exactly like lowering that one element by 1 would.
So each move can lower one element by 1 relative to the rest, and everything must come down to the minimum. Count the total amount above the minimum.
editorial: Adding 1 to n-1 elements keeps every pairwise difference between those elements and shifts the chosen element relative to them by -1. For the question of when all elements are equal only the differences matter, so the problem is the same as: in one move you may decrease a single element by 1, and you want all elements equal.

The cheapest common target is the current minimum, because lowering anything below it just costs more. Hence the answer is sum(nums) - n * min(nums). With the given limits this is at most 10,000 × 100,000 = 109, which fits in a 32-bit integer.
solution:
def minMoves(nums):
    return sum(nums) - len(nums) * min(nums)
